conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Dr. Martinez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health specialist who works with new mums and their families. You’ve already done the hardest part—getting here—so let’s take the next step together.

We’re going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger. My goal is to make sure you feel heard, supported, and that we figure out together what will help you feel more like yourself again.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no check-boxes or forms in front of you—and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Oh, yeah, I’ve still been laughing. Not like before-baby levels, but when my husband makes a dumb joke or when the baby does that startled little arm-flail thing, I chuckle. Maybe not every single day, but most days I can find something to smile at.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I mean, I’m not cracking up like I used to, but I still get a good laugh here and there. Yesterday my mom sent one of those silly cat videos and I actually laughed out loud while I was feeding the baby. So, I guess I’d say “yes, most of the time.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Actually… yeah, I do. Like, I’m excited for our weekly coffee run with my moms’ group on Thursday, and I’ve been planning a little outfit for the baby’s photo with Santa next week. I’m not bouncing-off-the-walls enthusiastic, but I still have stuff I look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. When the baby spit up all over the clean onesie right after I changed her, I just shrugged—it’s laundry, no big deal. If anything, I figure she’s a baby and these things just happen.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah… like I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, even though the monitor says she is. It’s not every minute, and I can usually tell myself “that’s just new-mom brain,” but the worry does pop up out of nowhere a couple of times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that “heart-racing, can’t-breathe” feeling. A couple of times my mind races when I think about SIDS or her getting sick, but it’s more a quick “what-if” thought than actual panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

Maybe a little, but nothing I can’t handle. Like, yesterday the dishes piled up and she wouldn’t nap unless I held her, so I felt a bit swamped for an hour. Once my husband got home and took over, I caught up and felt fine.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, sleeping’s actually one thing that’s going okay. Once I’m out, I’m out—usually get a four-hour chunk and then a couple of two-hour stretches. I’m tired, but it’s more physical tired from the day, not because my mind’s racing or I’m upset.
I have felt sad or miserable

I wouldn’t say “sad.” More like… tired and a little overwhelmed sometimes, but I haven’t had that heavy, gloomy feeling. I still enjoy my coffee and texting friends; I’m not walking around feeling miserable.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Hardly at all. Maybe once last week when I was super tired and she wouldn’t latch, I teared up for a minute, but I was over it as soon as she finally fed and fell asleep on my chest. Crying’s definitely not a daily thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel a little less worried and more rested, that’s all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms
- Intermittent, situational worry about infant safety (Q4), no pervasive anhedonia or persistent low mood (Q1-2, Q8)
- Denies excessive guilt, self-blame, or hopelessness (Q3)
- No panic episodes, but brief “what-if” catastrophic thoughts 2×/day (Q5)
- Mild, transient feeling of being “swamped,” readily relieved by support (Q6)
- Sleep disruption consistent with normal postpartum fatigue, not mood-related insomnia (Q7)
- Minimal tearfulness, quickly resolved (Q9)
- Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern
Predominantly mild, expectable new-mom anxiety without clear neurovegetative signs of depression. No functional impairment beyond typical childcare demands.

Screening significance
Overall score and clinical picture below threshold for major postpartum depression; monitor for escalation of anxiety or development of mood symptoms. Plan: routine 2-week check-in; psycho-education on self-care, support systems, and when to seek help.
